WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Environmental clearance to Upper Krishna Project 
*21. SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY: Will the Minister o f 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government of Karnataka had submitted proposals for 
environmental clearance to Upper Krishna Project, Stage- I, Phase -Ill, and 
Stage II in 1996; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether necessary clearance has been accorded; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(e) by when the clearance is likely to be granted? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (e) Proposals for environmental clearance in respect of 
Upper Krishna Project Stage- I, Phas e III, and Stage II were received from 
Government of Karnataka in September, 1996. In view of the dispute 
between Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh Governments regarding sharing of 
water from Krishna river, the project was referred to Ministry of Water 
Resources for their advice. 
Ministry of Water Resources informed this Ministry in May, 1997 that 
Planning Commission has given investment clearance to Upper Krishna 
Project Stage -I and, therefore, Phase III of Stage I could be considered for 
environmental clearance; Stage II may, however, be considered for clearance 
from environmental angle only after approval by the Technical Advisory 
Committee (TAC) of Ministry of Water Resources. TAC of Ministry of Water 
Resources has not yet approved Stage II of Upper Krishna Project. 
Hence, only the proposal for Stage I, Phase- Ill was examined in the 
Ministry. Based on the recommendations of the Expert Committee on River 
Valley and Hydroelectric Projects, the project authority was requested to 
submit details of the public hearing report in June, 1999. The details are still 
awaited. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [25 February, 2000] 
Grading System by CBSE 
*22. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister to HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have allowed Central Bo ard of Secondary 
Education to introduce grading system from the current/next year; and 
(b) whether other such Boards were consulted or the new policy is proposed 
to be imposed on them, once the CBSE pattern is implemented? 
' THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVE LOPMENT (DR. 
MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI): (a) and (b) The National Policy on Education 
has recommended the use of Grades in place of marks as one of the steps to 
recast the examination system. The Central Board of Secondary Education 
(CBSE), which is an autonomous organisation has taken a decision, in 
principle, to introduce the Grade System in declaration of results. 
In order to implement the decision, discussions are being held with various 
Schools, Teaching Community, Parents Representatives, Universities and 
other Boards. The question of imposing the Grade System by the CBSE on 
other Boards does not arise. The Council of Boards of School Education 
(COBSE), of which all the State Boards are members, in its Annual 
Conference held in December, 1999 have also recom mended introduction of 
Grading System for declaring results. 
Subsidy loss due to diversion of PDS foodgrains 
*23. SHRIMATI KAMLA SINHA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that substantial  portion of the subsidy continues to 
be lost because of diversion of P.D.S. foodgrains to the open market despite 
various measures taken to revampt the system; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof, stating the estimated annual loss of 
subsidy as a result thereof; 
4 

[25 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) what are the major causes identified by Government for failure to 
check diversion of P.D.S. foodgrains to open market; and 
(d) what measures are contemplated by Government to bring about 
improvement in the P.D.S. and check the diversions? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) The Tata Economic 
Consultancy Service (TECS) was engaged in the year 1997 for a study to 
assess the extent of diversion of foodgrains, sugar and edible oil from Public 
Distribution System (PDS) in the country. At the national level the diversion 
is estimated at 36% in case of wheat and 31% in case of rice. 
(b) The percentage of diversion with reference to the different targetted 
groups for whom there are different Central Issue Prices is not available from 
the study which was conducted around the time Targetted PDS was 
introduced. It is, therefore, not possible to quantify the loss of subsidy in 
monetary terms. 
(c) The major causes for diversion cited in the study are bulk diversion 
from godowns, bogus units in ration cards, underweighment at various 
levels, illiteracy of consumers, low profit margins for Fair Price Shops (FDS) 
owners, floating populations, fictitious distribution agencies, non -
availability/irregular supply and variation in entitlement and inferior quality 
with foreign particles. 
(d) Public Distribution System is implemented under the joint 
responsibility of the Central and State Governments/UT Administrations. 
The Central Government is responsible for p rocurement, storage and 
transportation of the PDS commodities up to the central godowns and 
making them available to the States. The responsibility for distribution to the 
consumers through the Fair Price Shops and administration of the PDS rests 
with the State Governments and UT Administrations. State Government have 
been requested to closely monitor PDS at the Fair Price Shops (FPSs) and 
other levels and to make arrangement for distribution of PDS commodities in 
a transparent and accountable manner by inv olvement of Panchayati Raj 
Institutions (PRIs) etc. in implementation of PDS. 
5 

RAJYA SABHA        [25 February, 2000] 
They have also been asked to eliminate bogus ration cards and initiate action 
against erring FPS owners under Section 3 of Essential Commodities Act, 
1955. 
The Government of India have set up Public Grievances' Redressal Cell in 
the Department of Public Distribution to attend to the complaints relating to 
any aspect of the Departments' functioning including the Public Distribution 
System. The Public Grievances' Redressal Cell has been provided with 
independent telephone, fax and e -mail facilities in addition to a facilitation 
counter to receive the public complaints. In order to attend to public 
complaints on priority, the Department has al so designated the senior officers 
of the Department as members of flying squad for conducting immediate and 
prompt enquiry whenever the need for it is felt. The Government of India also 
has appointed Area Officers to States/UTs to monitor the functioning o f 
Public Distribution System including the complaints of diversion. 
Seizure of Skins and Claws of Wild Animals 
*24. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a truck -load of skins of leopards, tigers, j ungle fox and 
other rare wild animals was seized in Ghaziabad on December 18 -19, 
1999; 
(b) if so, the details and the estimated cost of the catche; 
(c) whether any gang of smugglers and poachers has been caught and 
netted; if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) what steps have been taken and are being taken to curb the menace? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) One package containing skins of wild animals was seized from a 
truck carrying clothing at Ghaziabad on December 18-19, 1999. 
6 

[25 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the details are given in Statement -I (See below). It is difficult to 
ascertain the cost because these products are not consumed in the country. 
(c) Yes, Sir. The details are given in Statement-II (See below). 
(d) The steps taken to prevent poaching and illegal trade include: 
A Special Co -ordination Group has been set up in the Ministry with 
representatives of Ministry of Home, Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and 
the Central Bureau of Investigation to monitor anti -poaching activities and  
for taking effective measures in this regard. It has also been decided to hold 
meetings every 2 months of Chief Wildlife Wardens of sensitive States for 
the purpose of intelligence gathering and to take stock of anti -poaching 
measures. In order to - increase the effectiveness of these reviews, the State 
Police Officials are also being invited to these meetings. After the seizure of 
animal skins in Ghaziabad on December 19, 1999, 2 separate meetings of 
the-Chief Wildlife Wardens and one meeting of the Special Co -ordination 
Group have been held. Special measures have been taken with effect from 
June, 1999 to improve the effectiveness of the administration in protected 
areas as also to extend the protected area network by creation of 4 additional 
tiger reserves. Some of these measures include: 
- Availability of special funds to State Governments for  
creation of Strike Force to curb illegal activities in protected  
areas. 
— Special incentive for the officers and staff of tiger reserves who work 
in very harsh and difficult conditions. 
— Increase in compensation for cattle and human mortality due to wild 
animals. 
- Arrangement for training wildlife officers in the National 
Police Academy in intelligence gathering and crime 
investigation of wild offences. 
The Government of Uttar Pradesh has, on the request of the

Depletion of Forests in North-East 
*25. SHRI PRAFULL GORADIA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any scheme to stop depletion of forests, 
particularly in the North-East; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) whether Government are planning to have joint forest management 
schemes to ensure better involvement of the people? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) and (b) There are a number of Centrally Sponsore d Schemes, 
which contribute to regeneration, protection and development of forests in 
the country including the North- Eastern States and thus help to stop the 
depletion of forests. The total outlay for the Ninth Plan for the Ministry is 
Rs. 3013.84 crore out of which Rs. 380.50 crore is for Forestry sector, Rs. 
473.50 crore is for Wildlife Sector and Rs. 600 crore for National 
Afforestation and Eco -Development Board. It is proposed that from 2000-
2001, 10% of the Ministry's budget will be earmarked for deve lopment 
activity in the North -Eastern States. Plantation of bamboos is being 
encouraged in various States particularly in North-Eastern States. 
(c) As per the provisions of National Forest Policy, 1988, the Joint Forest 
Management programme is being implem ented in the country. For this 
purpose, the Government of India has issued guidelines to the various State 
Governments on the 1st June, 1990. So far the Joint Forest Management 
resolutions have been adopted in 22 States covering 10.25 million ha. of 
forests being managed by 36075 Joint Forest Management Committees 
(JFMC) in the country under this programme. To further strengthen the JFM 
approach, Government of India have issued fresh guidelines to the States on 
the 21st February, 2000.

RAJYA SABHA [25 February, 2000] 
Ban on consumption of Tobacco 
*26. SHRI RAJNATH SINGH 'SURYA':  
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that tobacco kills close to seven lakh people every 
year in India; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to ban tobacco products for those 
below 18 years; 
(c) whether any legislation is under consideration in this regard; 
(d) if so, the salient features thereof; and 
(e) whether it would also affect the sponsorship and advertisements by the 
Tobacco Industry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) As per the 
information furnished by Indian Council of Medical Research, a few 
community based surveys in India measured the mortality rates among 
tobacco-users and non- users to provide the excess risk of death among 
tobacco-users. Based on these studies and the death rate in India, an 
estimated eight lakhs deaths annually could be attributable to tobacco use. 
(b) to (e) The Committee on Subord inate Legislation (Tenth Lok Sabha) in 
its 22nd Report had made several recommendations primarily intended to 
discourage the use of tobacco and tobacco products. The Government is 
examining these recommendations and the draft legislation is under 
consideration of the Government.

Seizure of Deer Antlers 
*27. SHRI SOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY:  
   SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: 
Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government's attention ha s been drawn to the news -item 
appearing in Indian Express dated the 31st December, 1999, regarding 
seizure of three tonnes of deer antlers from poachers; 
(b) if so, the facts of the seizure revealed after probe; 
(c) how a massacre at such a huge scale went unnoticed; and 
(d) the measures proposed to check such trade? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T. R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Preliminary investigations conducted by the State Government have 
revealed that 3 tonnes of antlers seized belong to old stock of s hed antlers 
collected under license issued by the Chief Wildlife Warden, Uttar Pradesh.  
(c) Does not arise. As reported by the State Government, the antlers 
seized belong to the old stock of shed antlers that is shed by the deer as a part 
of biological process. 
(d) An order banning the collection of shed antlers has been issued by the 
Government of India.

New Revival Plan for IDPL 
*29. SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
SHRI GURUDAS DAS GUPTA: 
Will the Minister of CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are considering  a new revival plan for IDPL,

Self-reliant and export-oriented Drug Industry 
*37. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) the action taken to make the drug industry self -reliant and  export-
oriented; and 
(b) the investment and incentives proposed for vigorous research and 
break-through innovations to strengthen the Indian drug industry? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI 
SURESH PRABHU): (a) The action taken to make the drug i ndustry self -
reliant and export -oriented, inter alia, include: (i) setting up of the National 
Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research for training and 
educating research -oriented scientists; (ii) setting up of the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing  Authority, which is at an arm's length from the 
Government and fixing prices in transparent manner; (iii) setting up of an 
export cell in the Deptt. of Chemicals and Petrochemicals which is assisting 
pharmaceutical exporters; and (iv) prompt recognition to R and D centres in 
pharmaceutical companies. 
(b) The import incentives given for research and development, inter alia, 
include: (i) weighted tax deduction @ 125% for sponsored research 
programmes in approved national laboratories/universities etc.; (ii) a five -
year tax holiday to commercial R&D companies; (iii) exempting from price 
control a new drug which has not been produced elsewhere and which has 
been developed through indigenous R and D; and (iv) exemption from 
customs duty to research equipment imp orted by public funded and non -
commercial institutions.

WHO report on Tobacco Consumption 
*39. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether World Health Organisation has sent any report/ 
recommendation for controlling consumption of tobacco by law; and 
(b) if so, the salient features of WHO recommendations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N. T. SHANMUGAM): (a) and (b) The World 
Health Assembly vide its resolution dated 24th May, 1999 has urge d the 
member states: 
(i) To give high priority to accelerating work on development of the 
WHO framework convention on tobacco control and possible 
related protocols; 
(ii) To   provide   resources   and   co -operation   necessary   to 
accelerate the work; 
43 

RAJYA SABHA [25 February, 2000] 
(iii) To promote intergovernmental consultations to address specific 
issues, for example', public health matters and other technical 
matters relating to negotiation of the proposed WHO framework 
convention on tobacco control and possible related protocols; 
(iv) To establish, where appropriate, relevant structures, such as national 
commissions, for the WHO framework convention on tobacco 
control, and mechanisms to examine the implications of a 
framework convention on tobacc o control within the health and 
economic context, especially its effects in States where economy 
depends on agriculture; 
(v) To facilitate and support the participation of non governmental 
organisations, recognising the need for multisectoral representation; 
(vi) To consider further development and strengthening of national and 
regional tobacco policies, including the appropriate application of 
regulatory programmes to reduce tobacco use, as contributions to 
development of the framework convention and possi ble related 
protocols. 
The World Health Organisation has initiated steps for development of a 
global framework convention on tobacco control. The effort for Framework 
Convention On Tobacco Control (FCTC) is based on tobacco being a public 
health problem existing in every country; key elements like smuggling 
transcending national boundaries, and problem incapable of being fully 
tamed by countries acting in isolation. The first meeting of the Working 
Group constituted for this purpose was held on 25th to 29th  October 1999 at 
Geneva. The Working Group discussed and provided suggestions related to 
objectives and protocols for FCTC and also administrative arrangements for 
this purpose. The second meeting of the working group is scheduled to be 
held on 27th — 29th March, 2000 and based on the recommendations of the 
Working Group, Intergovernmental negotiating body will negotiate the draft 
framework convention and possible related protocols.

Production of nitrogenous and phosphatic fertilizers 
137. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in 1998 -99, the 13 MTs of nitrogenous and 
phosphatic fertilizers produced fell short of consumption by over 20 percent; 
and 
(b) if so, what actions Government are taking to achieve self -sufficiency 
in the same? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAMESH BAIS): (a) Total production of 
nitrogenous and phosphatic fertilizers du ring 1998-99 was 13.6 million tonnes 
as against the consumption of 15.46 million tonnes, which fell short of 
consumption by 12 percent. 
(b) India is almost self sufficient in urea with imports amounting to only 
about 2.8% of consumption in 1998-99. 
In the case of phosphates, the paucity of domestic raw material constrains 
the attainment of any degree of self -sufficiency. Recognising this, a 
deliberate policy -mix has been adopted which involves the modulation of 
three options: (i) domestic production based on indigenous/imported rock 
phosphate and imported sulphur; (ii) domestic production based on imported 
intermediates, viz. ammonia and phosphoric acid; and (iii) import of finished 
fertilizer, viz. Di-Ammonium Phosphate (DAP) and very rarely, Mono -
Ammonium Phosphate (MAP) and Nitrogen Phosphate Potash (NPK) 
complexes. Roughly 66% of the requirement of phosphatic fertilizers is met 
through the first two options. Since indigenous rock phosphate supplies meet 
only 5—10% of the total requirement of P 205, phosphatic fertilizers produced 
in the country are essentially based on imported raw materials and 
intermediates. 
There are no known commercially exploitable reserves of potash in the 
country and per force, the entire requirement of potassium 
46 

[25 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
fertilizers for direct application as well as for production of complex 
fertilizers is met through imports.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CHEMICALS 
AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAMESH BAIS): (a) and (b) Life saving nature

technology, etc. Treatment of T.B. is covered under a National Health 
Programme of the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare and medicines are 
distributed free to the needy, through the Government hospitals/dispensaries.

Vehicular Pollution in Major Cities 
190. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of  
ENVIORNMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that vehicular traffic is the most important source  
of pollution in all the major cities; 
(b) whether the level of pollution is increasing, inspite of the preventive 
measures being taken, due to unrestricted growth of vehicular traffic; and 
(c) if so, in what manner Government plan to control this situation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) Yes, Sir. Vehicular 
traffic is a major source of air pollution in all the major cities. 
(b) The air pollution levels have increased in metropolitan cities. However, 
in cas e of Delhi, the Central Pollution Control Board has reported that air 
pollution load has decreased in 1998-99. 
(c) The measures taken/proposed to be taken to control the pollution 
include notification of stringent emission norms, improvements in fuel 
quality a nd vehicle technology, phasing out of old commercial vehicles, 
promotion of' use of clean fuel, augmentation of public transport system, 
optmisation of traffic flow and development of road infrastructure.

Reduction of pollution from smoke and dust 
197. SHRI PRA NAB MUKHERJEE: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any research has been undertaken for reduction of air  
pollution by smoke and dust; 
(b) if so, with what results and if not, whether the Ministry would  
initiate such a research; and 
(c) what measures are being enforced for protection of  
environment from pollution by fly-ash? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS (SHRI BABU LAL MARANDI): (a) and (b) Smoke and 
dust in the air result from seve ral sources like vehicular exhaust, emissions 
from industries like cement, petroleum fertilizer, chemical etc., mining, 
construction activities, thermal power plants and so on Deforestation also 
leads to wind erosion and resultant dust in the air. Research  studies have been 
carried by various scientific organisations including Central/ State agencies, 
NGOs and private companies in their respective areas. To cite a few 
examples, research studies are progressing to develop slurry -based transport 
system for fl y-ash in place of dry transport system, development of various 
products from fly-ash, improvement in 2T oil to reduce smoke and particulate 
matter from 2T stroke engine, as also change of 2 -stroke engines to 4 -stroke 
engines, phasing out more than 15 -years old vehicles from metropolitan cities 
use of bag house technology to reduce suspended particulate matter pollution, 
raising of green belts of identified plant species around factories, to reduce air 
pollution, intensive afforestation measures in urban and  deforested/desert 
lands etc. Air 
120 

[25 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
pollution studies are among the priority R&D areas of the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests which will continue to support research in this 
sector. 
(c) Utilization of fly -ash is being  promoted for manufacture of products 
such as bricks, concrete blocks cement, ceramic tiles material for 
construction of roads, dams, dykes, etc. It is also being used in the 
agricultural sector as soil amendment and for preparation of urea- fly-ash 
pellets as slow release nitrogen fertilizer. It is also being used for wasteland 
reclamation and filling the mine pits. 
The Ministry of Environment and Forests, vide notification No. S.O. 763(E) 
dt. 14.9.99, issued under Environment Protection Act, 1986 has made it 
compulsory for the brick manufacturers within a radius of 50 KMs from coal 
or lignite base thermal power plants to use 25% of fly -ash with soil on 
weight to weight basis. Government agencies like CPWD, PWD, 
development authorities, housing boards, National Highway Authority of 
India and other Construction agencies have been asked to prescribed the use 
of. ash and ash-based products in their construction applications. 
Fly-ash Mission has also been constituted by the Government of India during 
August 1994 with Deptt. of Science and Technology as the nodal agency and 
Technology Information, Forecasting Council (TIFAC) as the implementing 
agency. The mission works in close cooperation with other agencies like 
Ministry of Environment and Forests, Ministry of P ower, Thermal Power 
Stations, NTPC, R&D institutions, academia and industry. It has major focus 
on technology demonstration projects for developing confidence in fly -ash 
technologies for large -scale adoptions. Thrust areas identified under the 
mission incl ude characterisation of fly -ash, hydraulic structures; handling 
and transportation; ash ponds and dams; agriculture - related studies and 
applications; reclamation of ash ponds for human settlement, roads and 
embankments, underground mine fills, building co mponents, and research 
projects.

Tuberculosis Eradication Programmes with the assistance of international 
agencis;

programmes according to the convenience of the poor patients; and

Appraisal of Malaria Eradication Programme 
210. SHRIMATI KAMLA SINHA: Will the Minister of H EALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have made any recent appraisal of the Centrally 
sponsored Malaria Eradication Scheme to know the achievements since its 
inception; 
(b) if so, what are the details thereof; and 
(c) what strategy is contemplated by Government in the light of 
153 
 

RAJYA SABHA [25 February, 2000] 
the  implementation of the scheme  and  the deficiencies,  if any, identified? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) to (c) Critical 
Appraisal / review of the National Anti Malaria Programme (NAMP) have 
been carried out by way of Constitution of Committees/Task Forces since its 
inception and based on the recommendations of the Committees, necessary 
modifications made in the Programme from time to time. During December, 
1994 the Programme was reviewed by the Hon'ble Prime Minister and an 
Expert Committee on Malaria appointed to identify the problem areas and 
formulate specific strategies to tackle the problem in such areas. Taking into 
account the recommendation of the Expert Committee, Malaria Action 
Programme (MAP) was formulated and implemented since 1995. 
Further, Performance Appraisal of the NAMP for the period from 1992 to 
1997 was conducted by the Comptroller & Auditor General (C&AG) of India. 
While expressing satisfaction on the Annual Blood Examination Rate 
(ABER), the C&AG in their report —Union Government (Civil) for the year 
ended March, 1998 inter -alia mentioned that incidence of malaria during the 
period remained between 21.26 lakhs to 30.36 lakhs. 
The report further speaks about shortfall in spray operations, delay in 
providing presumptive and radical treatment in some cases and shortage of 
staff in the States thereby affecting implementation of the Programme. 
The findings / observations in the report of the C&AG have been shared 
with the State Governments. 
In view of the prevailing malaria situation, an Enhanced Malaria Control 
Project (EMCP) with World Bank support essentially covering 100 tribal 
predominant highly malaria endemic districts of 7 peninsular States namely 
Andhra Pradesh, Bihar, Orissa, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and 
Rajasthan and 19 cities/towns having high endemicity of Malaria in these 
States and in the State of 
154 

[25 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Karnataka, Tamil Nadu & West Bengal is being implemented since 
September, 1997 to intensify malaria control activities by way of additional 
inputs through a mix of interventions as under:—  
* Early case Detection and Prompt Treatment (EDPT) through use of 
newer drugs and Rapid Diagnostic kits. 
* Selective Vector Control including use of Synthetic Pyrethroids in rural 
areas and Biolarvicides in urban areas. 
* Promotion of personal protection methods by use of Medicated Mosquito 
Nets (MMS). 
* Early detection and containment of epidemics. 
* Information, Education and Communication towards personal 
prevention and Community participation. 
* Institutional and Management capacity building manpower 
development through intensive re -orientation training programmes at all 
levels and efficient Management Information System (MIS). 
Annual Programme Development Review (APDR) is an integral part of the 
EMCP.

Charges Against MNC Toothpastes 
212. SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the report titled "Beware of MNC 
toothpastes: CDA" which appeared in the Economic Times dated February 1, 
2000; 
(b) if so, whether Government have studied the report and referred it to 
the Dental Council of India to elicit a medical appraisal of these charges as 
most of the brands mentioned by the CDA report are very much in vogue in 
India; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) According to Dental Council of India, the Organising Committee of 
the Commonwealth Dental Association (CDA) and the Indian Dental 
Association (IDA) has denied having issued a Press release, expressing 
concern about the quality of multinational toothpaste brands in developing 
countries. In fact, the CDA -IDA release m entioned that the Congress has 
highlighted the benefit of using a good quality toothpaste for cleaning teeth 
and noted the beneficial qualities of multinational brands available in India.  
(c) and (d) Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, toothpastes are 
considered as 'Cosmetic', the standards for which have been 
156 

[25 February, 2000]        RAJYA SABHA 
prescribed under Schedule 'S' of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 which 
require the manufactures to conform to the Indian Standard specifications 
laid down for the purpose by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS).

Curbing tobacco consumption 
215. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister  of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether WHO has stressed the need to develop and implement 
tobacco control strategies; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to bring forth any legislation to 
restrict use of tobacco; 
(c) whether the tobacco related diseases are increasing in the country and 
if so, the total number of persons died due to such diseases during the last 
three years; and 
(d) what other strategies would be adopted to curb use of tobacco in the 
country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) Yes, Sir. WHO has 
initiated steps for development of a global framework convention on tobacco 
control and has stressed need for implementation of tobacco control 
activities by all the members States. 
(b) to (d) The committee on Subordinate Legislation (Tenth Lok Sabha) in 
its 22nd Report had made several recommendations primarily intended to 
discourage the use of tobacco and its products. The Government is 
examining these recommendations and the draft legislation is under 
consideration of the Government. As per data furnished by Indian Council of 
Medical Research, the year -wise trends related to mortality and morbidity 
due to tobacco use in India arc not available. However, it has been estimated 
that in India about eight lakhs deaths occur due to tobacco use. Currently, an 
estimated 163000 new cases of cancer occur in India in a year, due to 
tobacco 
173 

RAJYA SABHA [25 February, 2000] 
use. The estimated number of cases of coronary artery disease and chronic 
obstructive lung diseases due to tobacco use in India are 44.5 lakhs and 39.2 
lakhs, respectively.

Allopathic medicines  vis-a-vis other systems 
217. SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE:  
MISS MABEL REBELLO: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Allopathic system of medicines is comparatively expensive 
than other systems such a s Homoepathic medicines, Ayurvedic, Unani and 
Herbal systems of medicines; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Allopathic medicines are not only most 
expensive, but also have more side- effects than other systems of medicines 
practised in India; and 
(c) whether Government have been continuously encouraging the use of 
Allopathic medicines, by establishing more medical colleges, hospitals, health 
centres and sub -health centres for such purpose, whereas other systems of 
medicines are not equally encouraged; if so, why? 
THE M INISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI N.T. SHANMUGAM): (a) The cost of 
medicines depends on many factors, including overall cost of therapy, 
availability of drugs and also research and development. As such, it can not 
be gener alised that Allopatthic System of Medicine, is comparatively 
expensive than other systems of medicines. 
(b) The side effects are seen both with Allopathic System of Medicines 
and other system of medicines. It is not possible to compare the incidence of 
side effect with both the systems. However, such effects are well documented 
over the years and well known to the practitioners in Allopathic System of 
Medicines. 
(c) Government is eqully encouraging all the systems of medicines 
depending on the requirement and deman ds of the patients and infrastructure 
available.

The major amendments made in the Admission guidelines inter -alia, 
provide for according higher priority to the children of Central Government 
employees including Defence personnel over other employees, 3% 
reservation for the handicapped children, placing 10 seats in each section of

discretion of the chairman, VMC, prescribing upper age limit for admission at 
minimum age + 2 years, etc. 
Transfer Guidelines 
• Transfer Guidelines now seek to quantify the parameters  
usually taken into account while effecting the transfers. In  
broad terms, these parameters are organisational reasons/  
interests and needs of the persons  seeking transfer. While  
considering organisational reasons/interests as an element of  
transfer policy, due emphasis has been given for performance  
of the teachers as also for their mobility from NE region,  
Sikkim, A&N Islands and listed hard stations. Lik ewise, 
grounds on which teachers seek transfer have also been  
quantified. These grounds are completion of tenure in  
specified areas, blind & orthopadically handicapped, spouse  
cases etc. 
. In order to accommodate teachers who have completed their  
tenure in NE Region, Sikkim, A&N Islands and listed hard  
stations and other teachers who have not been able to get  
places of their choice for 5 years or more, a provision has  
been made to transfer them to places of their choice by  
transferring out teachers with longest stay at those stations. 
• Entitlement points have been fixed for organisational reasons/ interests 
as also for needs of the individuals on the basis of which transfer is 
sought. 
• Cases of transfer sought on account of death of spouse or serious 
illness h ave been kept out of the aforesaid scale system. These cases 
would be placed enbloc higher than the others in terms of priority. 
• Transfer TA would now be regulated as per orders of the Government 
of India on the subject. 
• A provision has been made to initia te disciplinary proceedings and 
disqualify the teachers bringing political and outside pressure in the 
matter of transfer. 
 
190 

[25 February, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
• Guidelines as prescribed for teachers would mutatis-mutandis be 
applicable to non-teaching staff also. 
Need and Justification for Amendments 
The changes in admission guidelines were necessitated to bring the 
admission priorities in consonance with the objectives of KVS and also to 
bring about the over -all improvement in the admission process. The 
amendments in Transfer Guidelines were made with a view to provide a 
better degree of satisfaction to the teachers posted in NE Region/difficult 
areas and other places which are not of their choice as also to ensure greater 
degree of objectivity in the matter of transfers.

(i)    The work of  track circuiting has been accelerated on the trunk 
routes and other important main lines,

minimize chances of human errors in causing accidents,  
(iii)  Auxiliary warning system for  giving advance warning about 
'signal at danger' to the driver of the running train has been 
commissioned on Mumbai suburban sections,

ballast cleaning machines for track maintenance. 
(vii) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of    
the    track,    sophisticated    track    recording    car s, 
oscillograph cars and portable accelerometer are being 
progressively used. 
(viii)  For detecting rail  fractures and weld failure 96 more double 
rail Ultra Sonic Flaw Detectors are being procured. 
(ix)   In addition to the above, 2 Self Propelled Ultra Sonic Rail 
Testing Cars are also being procured,  
(x)  Maintenance facilities for coaches and wagons have been 
modernised and upgraded at many depots,

been equipped with ultrasonic testin g equipment for detection 
of flaws in the axles.

(e) Steps taken to prevent accidents are given as below:—  
(i) The work of track circuiting has been accelerated on the trunk routes 
and other important main lines, 
(ii) Modification of the signaling circuitry is being carried out to minimize 
chances of human errors in causing accidents. 
(iii) Auxiliary warning system for giving advance warning about 'signal at 
danger' to the driver of the running train has been commissioned on 
Mumbai suburban sections. 
(iv) Railway Board has cleared a pilot project of AWS for Tughlaqabad -
Mathura section of Central railway on a trial basis. 
(v) Walkie-Talkie sets have been supplied to Drivers and Guards of all 
Passenger carrying trains. The same is presently being supplied to 
Drivers and Guards of goods trains also and the same is likely to be 
completed by 31st March, 2000. 
(vi) There has bee n progressive increase in use of Tie Tamping and 
ballast clearning machines for track maintenance. 
(vii) For monitoring track geometry and running characteristics of the 
track, sophisticated track recording cars, oscillograph cars and 
portable accelerometer are being progressively used. 
(viii) For detecting rail fractures and weld failure, 96 more double rail 
Ultra Sonic Flaw Detectors are being procured. 
(ix) Maintenance facilities for coaches and wagons have been modernised 
and upgraded at many depots. 
(x) To prevent cases of cold breakage of axles, ROH Depots have been 
equipped with ultrasonic testing equipment for detection of flaws in 
the axles. 
(xi) Whistle boards/speed breakers and road signs have been provided at 
unmanned level crossings and visibili ty for drivers has been 
improved. 
247

(xii) Audio -visual publicity campaigns to educate road users on how to 
make a safe crossing are conducted. 
(xiii) Steps have been taken to prevent inflammable and explosive 
materials from being carried in passenger trains. 
(xiv) Periodic Safety Audit of different divisions by inter disciplinary 
teams from zonal headquarters has been introduced. 
(xv) Training facilities for drivers, guards and staff connected with train 
operation have bee n modernized including use of simulators for 
training of drivers. 
(xvi) Refresher courses are regularly organized at specified intervals. 
(xvii) Performance of the staff connected with train operations is being 
constantly monitored and those found deficien t are sent for crash 
training. 
(xviii) Periodical safety drives are conducted to inculcate safety 
consciousness among the staff.
